summary: Supplements RFC 3279 with encoding formats, identifiers and parameter formats for the GOST R 34.10-94, GOST R 34.10-2001 and GOST R 34.11-94 algorithms in X.509 certificates and CRLs. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Tells certificate makers how to write down the details of the GOST signing methods on a digital ID card.

subtitle: How to write GOST signatures, hashes and public keys into X.509 certificates and CRLs.

tldr.problem: The Russian GOST signature and hash algorithms had no agreed identifiers or encodings for Internet X.509 certificates and CRLs, so products from different vendors could not interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines object identifiers, parameter structures, signature and public key encodings, and keyUsage rules for GOST R 34.10-94, GOST R 34.10-2001 and GOST R 34.11-94.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that supplements RFC 3279, giving the Russian Cryptographic Software Compatibility Agreement community one common certificate format.

today: RFC 4491 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2006. It updates RFC 3279, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
This RFC supplements RFC 3279. It describes how to use the GOST R 34.10-94 and GOST R 34.10-2001 signature algorithms, the VKO key derivation algorithms and the GOST R 34.11-94 one-way hash function in the Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure (PKI).

It exists to give the "Russian Cryptographic Software Compatibility Agreement" community the extra information and specifications it needs. The document defines the contents of the signatureAlgorithm, signatureValue, signature and subjectPublicKeyInfo fields in certificates and CRLs, and the allowed keyUsage values for each algorithm. The ASN.1 modules live in a separate document (RFC 4357).

It does not restate the algorithms themselves. The full GOST specifications are referenced (in Russian), and CAs and applications MUST support at least one of the specified public key and signature algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a filling-in guide for one kind of digital ID card. The secret math is written down somewhere else; this guide only says where each piece goes on the card.

sections.title: The GOST R 34.11-94 Hash
sections.content:
GOST R 34.11-94 is a one-way, collision-free hash function. It produces a 256-bit hash value from an input of any finite bit length. The RFC says it is the only hash function that can be used with the GOST R 34.10-94/2001 signature algorithms.

The function MUST always be used with the parameter set identified by id-GostR3411-94-CryptoProParamSet. What data is hashed when signing certificates and CRLs is described in RFC 3280.
sections.plainLanguage: A hash is like squashing any size of story into a short fingerprint. If even one word changes, the fingerprint changes, so you can tell someone tampered with it.

sections.title: Signature Algorithms and Their Encoding
sections.content:
A CA may use GOST R 34.10-94 or GOST R 34.10-2001 to sign certificates and CRLs, and these MUST always be paired with GOST R 34.11-94. Each combination has its own object identifier: id-GostR3411-94-with-GostR3410-94 and id-GostR3411-94-with-GostR3410-2001. In the AlgorithmIdentifier the parameters field SHALL be omitted, so it is a SEQUENCE of just the identifier.

Both algorithms produce a signature made of two 256-bit numbers. Its octet string form is 64 octets: the first 32 hold s in big-endian form and the second 32 hold r' (for the 1994 algorithm) or r (for the 2001 algorithm).

Certificates and CRLs store signatures as bit strings, so the octet string must be converted. The most significant bit of the first octet becomes the first bit of the bit string, and so on to the last bit of the last octet.
sections.plainLanguage: The signature is two big numbers glued together in a set order. To put them on the card you copy them bit by bit, in order, into a long row of ones and zeros.

sections.title: Public Key Identifiers and Parameters
sections.content:
A GOST R 34.10-94 public key is identified by id-GostR3410-94 and a GOST R 34.10-2001 key by id-GostR3410-2001. The SubjectPublicKeyInfo.algorithm.algorithm field MUST be set to the matching identifier. The same key can serve for signatures or for the VKO key derivation algorithm, but using one key for both is NOT RECOMMENDED.

The parameters field MAY be omitted or set to NULL. Otherwise it MUST be a SEQUENCE of three parts: publicKeyParamSet, digestParamSet and an encryptionParamSet that defaults to id-Gost28147-89-CryptoPro-A-ParamSet. The parameter sets themselves are defined in RFC 4357.

If the parameters are absent they are inherited from the issuer certificate, as RFC 3280 describes. When the working_public_key_parameters variable ends up null, the certificate and any signature verifiable on it SHALL be rejected.
sections.plainLanguage: The card says which kind of key this is and, optionally, which settings go with it. If the settings are left off, you borrow them from the card of whoever issued it, and if there are none to borrow, the card is thrown out.

sections.title: How the Public Keys Are Encoded
sections.content:
Each public key MUST be DER-encoded as an OCTET STRING, and that encoding is used as the contents of the subjectPublicKey BIT STRING.

  • GOST R 34.10-94: the key Y = a^x (mod p) is 128 octets in little-endian form.
  • GOST R 34.10-2001: the key is a point Q = (x,y) on an elliptic curve, 64 octets: the first 32 hold x and the second 32 hold y, both little-endian.

Some applications wrongly drop zero bits at the end of the BIT STRING. The RFC RECOMMENDS padding with zeroes on decoding, up to 1048 bits (131 octets) for GOST R 34.10-94 keys and 528 bits (66 octets) for GOST R 34.10-2001 keys, so the inner octet string can still be decoded.
sections.plainLanguage: The key is written as a fixed-length row of bytes. Since some programs chop off empty bits at the end, readers are told to put them back before reading.

sections.title: Key Usage Rules
sections.content:
If a keyUsage extension is present in an end-entity certificate holding a GOST key, it MAY contain digitalSignature, nonRepudiation, keyEncipherment and keyAgreement. When keyAgreement or keyEncipherment is present, encipherOnly and decipherOnly MAY also appear, but the extension MUST NOT assert both.

In a CA or CRL signer certificate the allowed values are digitalSignature, nonRepudiation, keyCertSign and cRLSign. The same constraints apply to GOST R 34.10-2001 keys as to GOST R 34.10-94 keys.
sections.plainLanguage: A card can say what its key is allowed to do, such as sign letters or lock secrets. The rules list which jobs may be written on which kind of card.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Applications are RECOMMENDED to verify that signature values and subject public keys conform to the GOST standards before using them.

If a certificate stands in for a handwritten signature under the Russian Federal Electronic Digital Signature Law, it MUST contain a keyUsage extension, that extension MUST be critical, and it MUST NOT include keyEncipherment or keyAgreement.

CAs and applications are also RECOMMENDED to make sure a signing private key is not used beyond its allowed validity period, typically 15 months for both signature algorithms. For discussion of algorithm parameters, the RFC points to the security section of RFC 4357.
sections.plainLanguage: Check the signature before you trust it. A card used like a handwritten signature must say, in a way nobody can ignore, that it is only for signing, and the signing key should not be used for too long.

sections.title: Example Certificates
sections.content:
The RFC closes with two complete example certificates in PEM form, each followed by a dump of its ASN.1 structure: one signed with GOST R 34.10-94 and one with GOST R 34.10-2001. Both use the example subject name with organization CryptoPro and country RU.

The dumps show the signature algorithm identifier, the public key algorithm with its two parameter identifiers, and the key and signature as bit strings. The text also lists the numbers inside them (r' and s, or x, y, the private key d, r and s), which implementers can use to check their encoders and decoders.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two finished sample cards, one for each method. You can compare your own work against them to see if you did it right.
